passages.quote:
This guide is for UK-qualified professionals and businesses who want to understand how to get their UK professional qualifications recognised internationally (including in North, Central and Latin America, Africa, Middle East, Asia, Australia, New Zealand and wider Europe).

For guidance on providing services in the EU, read ‘Recognition of UK professional qualifications in EU member states’. Recognition requirements and processes vary by country and by profession.

This guidance explains the typical steps, where to find authoritative information, and what to prepare before you contact the relevant overseas regulator or competent authority.

Overview

What recognition means

Some professions are regulated in law. This means there is a legal requirement to have your professional qualifications (and sometimes your experience) assessed before you can carry out certain professional activities or use a protected professional title, like ‘architect’.

In most countries, recognition decisions are made by the overseas regulator or ‘competent authority’ for that profession. There is no single international system for recognition, so you will usually need to check requirements for your specific profession and the country (or region) where you want to work. You may also need to meet separate requirements for registration and licensure, such as visas or work permits.

This guidance is focused on recognition of professional qualifications (RPQ) and does not replace advice from overseas regulators, employers or immigration authorities.

Before you start:

confirm the country where you want to work. If the country has a federalised regulation system (for example, some licensing is set at state or provincial level), be prepared to check rules for the specific state, province, territory or region where you will work

be clear about the professional activities you want to carry out and the title you want to use

confirm whether you will provide services temporarily, occasionally, or on a long-term basis (requirements can differ)

gather evidence of your UK qualifications, your UK professional registration, your work experience and qualifications from the relevant UK competent authority or chartered/professional membership body – you may need to provide copies of these to confirm your qualifications and registration status

allow time and budget for fees, translations, certification of documents and (in some cases) tests or adaptation periods

check whether you need to meet language requirements

Step 1: check whether your profession is regulated in your target country

Not every profession is regulated in every country. In some places you can work without having your qualification formally recognised, but you may still need to meet other requirements (for example, visa/work requirements, employer checks, licensing rules, or membership of a professional body).

Check:

the target country’s government websites for information on regulated professions and licensing

websites of the overseas regulator or professional body for your profession

If the country has multiple jurisdictions (for example, federal systems), check requirements for the specific state, province or region.

Trade associations, chambers of commerce and employers may be able to point you to the correct regulator, but you should still verify requirements with the regulator directly.

Step 2: identify the overseas regulator or competent authority

If your profession is regulated, you will usually need to apply to the overseas regulator or competent authority to have your qualifications assessed. In some countries, there may be different bodies for registration, licensing, and professional conduct.

In countries with federal or devolved systems, regulation can be set at state, provincial or territorial level. This can mean there is more than one competent authority, depending on where you plan to work.

When you contact the overseas regulator, ask what you need to do to practise your profession in that country.

For example, ask about:

whether your UK qualifications are eligible for assessment

the application route (for example, for experienced professionals, new graduates, or temporary services)

documents you must provide (and whether they must be certified or translated)

fees and expected processing times

any exams, interviews, supervised practice or adaptation periods

language requirements

how to appeal or request a review if your application is refused

Step 3: check whether any recognition arrangement is available

In some cases, there may be bilateral recognition arrangements that make it easier to have your UK qualification recognised overseas. These can include Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs) between regulatory or professional bodies, or other arrangements such as memoranda of understanding (MoUs).

Some UK trade agreements include frameworks to support recognition discussions between regulators, but recognition decisions are still made by the overseas regulator. You should check with the regulator what, if any, arrangement applies to your profession. See Annex 1 for a select list of arrangements that UK regulated sectors have with international partners, and Annex 2 for a list of broader country-level agreements.

You can also read ‘Arrangements to facilitate the recognition of professional qualifications’ for background on different types of arrangements.

Step 4: prepare your evidence and apply

Most regulators will have an application process for overseas-qualified professionals. You may need to apply online, pay a fee, and provide documents to show your identity, qualifications and professional experience.

Common documents can include:

your passport or other identity documents

qualification certificates and transcripts

evidence of professional registration or membership in the UK (if applicable)

references, employment history, or evidence of practice hours
